Discusses the Sabha Parab (14 chapters) and quotes from it; notes the manuscript in the Maharaja of Patiala's collection.
Gives samples of Amrit Rai's verse in various meters alongside the Sabha Parab discussion.
Quotes the colophon of Mangal's Shalya Parab (Anandpur, 1753 Bk) and says the manuscript is in the Moti Bagh Library, Patiala.
Prints Mangal's verse petition to Mata Jito, asking leave to go to Pasrur for his daughter's wedding, copied from an old Dasam Granth manuscript.
Collects samples of Mangal's kabitts on various subjects, including verses on the Guru and Anandpur.

Padam's discussion of the work and its authorship.
Padam's discussion of the works attributed to Mani Singh.
Padam's chapter on Nanua quotes his padas with raga headings (e.g. Kidara, Asavari); it notes that the asavaris are in plain Panjabi and the rest in Sant-bhasha.
Padam discusses Hans Ram's Karan Parab (begun 1752 Bk, rewarded with 60,000 takas) and quotes passages, including the opening; this is the only published sample.
Padam's Hans Ram chapter quotes his verse, including stanzas praising Guru Gobind Singh; this is the only published sample of Hans Ram's other poetry.
Padam quotes Kunvresh's Dron Parab, including the colophon naming Anandpur on the Sutlej and the poet's home at Bari.
Padam describes Kunvresh's Samudrik (98 chhands), quotes its opening and last verses, and locates it in Sikh Reference Library MS 5025, which Bal Chand Fateh Gobind copied at Anandpur in 1753 Bk.
Padam describes Kunvresh's 'Rati Rahas Kok' (7 chapters, 279 chhands), which he saw with Giani Karnail Singh of Amritsar, and quotes stanzas in praise of the Gurus.
Padam quotes Tahkan's Asvamedh Parab, including the verses where the poet names himself (Chopra, Jalalpur), and notes its 1726 Bk date and that it does not praise the Guru.
Padam describes Tahkan's Ratan Dam (an Amarakosha rendering in 28 prabhavs and about 1,420–1,426 chhands) and quotes its opening and verses mentioning the Guru.
Padam's Tahkan chapter ends with a 'Phutkal chhand' section quoting his miscellaneous verses; this is the only published sample.
Padam's Tahkan section prints Panjabi songs under raga headings such as Tilang Kafi and Bilaval, signed 'Tahkan'.
Padam quotes the couplet in Chand's Udyog Parab where he says he first rendered the Karan Parab; he suggests Hans Ram's version was adopted instead.
Padam quotes Chand's Udyog Parab ('Udam Parab') and says its manuscript is in the Moti Bagh (Patiala royal) library.
Padam lists 'Prichha Guru Gobind Singh' among Chand's works, but the sample found shows no extract from it.
Padam lists Chand's 'Triya Charitra' and draws on Chand's charitras for Mughal-era detail; this is the best published lead to the poet's own text.
Padam prints Chand's guru-mahima kabitts and chhappays collected from various manuscripts.
Padam discusses Ani Rai and his account of the clash with imperial troops in the Jangnama.
Padam's Sukhdev chapter discusses Adhyatam Prakash (colophon 1755 Bk) and quotes it.
Padam lists 'Chhand Vichar Pingal (1728 Bk)' among Sukhdev's works and discusses it with his other prosody writing.
Padam treats 'Brind' as a court poet and says the Satsai explicitly mentions the Guru and Anandpur, completed in Kattak 1761 Bk.

Padam's Brind chapter lists Bhav Panchashika and cites a Gurmukhi copy at Bhasha Vibhag Library, Patiala (MS 201) whose colophon calls Brind a court poet of Guru Gobind Singh; it quotes from the Satsai only, not this work (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam lists 'Shringar Shiksha' among Brind's works; no text is reproduced (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam's list of Brind's works gives the title 'Hitopadesh Shatak' that the book cites; no text quoted (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam's list gives the title as 'Pavath Pachisi' (6th of Brind's works); no text quoted (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam lists 'Yamakalankar' as Brind's 6th work without quoting it (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam prints Pingal Sar's opening, the author's genealogy and its colophon (308 stanzas, Agra, S.1745) from Bhasha Vibhag Library, Patiala, MS 129, including a doha naming Guru Gobind Singh (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Gives Alam's kabitt praising the Guru, plus a kabitt, a savaiya and two Panjabi kafis in Rag Jaijaivanti and Rag Jaitsri, which match the book's description (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

contains.note: Prints the full Kharkha in Rag Todi (13 stanzas, Bhangani to Chamkaur) from Sikh Reference Library MS 3547 (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam gives the one Panjabi viraha stanza signed 'Nand Ram' found in Gurmukhi MSS and mentions his 'Nand Ram Pachisi' (1687) on the Kali age (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam attributes the work to the scribe Haridas (1693) and prints the colophon and the opening prologue on prema (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam lists Panchtantra among Dharam Singh's works; the family told him their manuscripts of it and of Gurbilas were taken by a sadhu and never returned (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam calls Dharam Singh's work 'Kok Sar': prose in 14 chapters opening with a savaiya invoking Chandi, which he quotes, and lists 'Kok Sanvad' among his works (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

contains.locator: p. 188: Katha Raje Bharthari Hari Ki
contains.note: Padam records the Katha's manuscript at Moti Bagh Library, Patiala (MS 139), and quotes its opening doha (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam identifies 'Var Patshahi Dasvin Ki' as the Var appended to Bhai Gurdas's vars, quotes pauri 1, and argues that only the first 14 pauris are original (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam names two manuscripts: Sikh Reference Library MS 1191, which has both the Var and the Baramah, and Central Public Library, Patiala, MS 2743. He gives the closing doha and says the poem is on Bharat's separation from Rama (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Padam says Gurdas Singh wrote prayay (glosses) on the Guru Granth Sahib that were never printed (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Prints Bhai Pheru's bhajans in Rag Suhi Lalit, Sham Kalyan, Kanra and Todi, which match the book's description (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam gives four kabitts in praise of the Guru (gur-mahima) found in manuscripts, and notes that only Mahima Prakash names Brahm Bhatt among the court poets (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Gives Hir Bhatt's martial poems, twelve kabitts, a savaiya and a chhappay, with the anecdote of his recitation at court (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Three kabitts praising Guru Gobind Singh; Padam suggests the poet may be the Gwalior Sundardas, author of 'Sundar Shringar' (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Two kabitts by Sharda, one comparing the Guru's staff to Krishna's flute (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
A single kabitt in which the poor poet casts himself as Sudama before the Guru as Gobind/Krishna (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Padam mentions Husain's kabitt on Guru Nanak's rabab without quoting it, and prints four Sufi-style lines, in what he admits is modern-sounding language, that Jathedar Sham Singh had copied from an old pothi (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

Gives Chandan's riddling 'navsat' savaiya, solved at court by Dhanna Singh, and one more kabitt, and suggests he is the Chandan Rai killed at Chamkaur (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).
Gives Dhanna Singh's riddle savaiya, which Chandan failed to answer, and the exchange with Chandan (mirror scan: archive.org/details/darbari-ratan-piara-singh-padam).

versions.label: Padam, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji de Darbari Ratan (Patiala 1976)

contains.note: Padam's entry on Ramdas gives his one surviving piece, a kafi in Rag Suhi, with a note that Baba Sumer Singh and Giani Gian Singh count him among the court poets. Page 208 is scan leaf n211.

Padam quotes the Sanskrit shloka Pandit Brij Lal recited before the Guru, with a Panjabi gloss. He takes it from Gurpratap Suraj Granth, Rut 5, Ansu 27, and adds that Brij Lal may also have written in Hindi. Page 209 is scan leaf n212.

Prints the Bhangani pauris credited to the dhadi Mir Chhabila (Guru Gobind Singh's victory over the hill chiefs). Padam refers to his separate study Varan Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji Kian (1962). Page 210 is scan leaf n213.

Padam writes that a single karkha (kharkha-metre piece) survives from Mushki and quotes it, describing it as a martial-metre battle piece of the kind sung in vars. This confirms the row's 'kharkha meter'. Page 211 is scan leaf n214.

Padam identifies Desa Singh as a son of Kesho Bhatt and prints his pauris praising the Guru, sung at a wedding in Bhai Mani Singh's family (c. 1750 Bk). This fits the row's wedding poem. Page 214 is scan leaf n217.
Padam calls Kirat Singh perhaps the first scholar at the court to write a Prayay (glossary/commentary) of the Guru Granth Sahib and links him with Bhai Mani Singh. Page 216 is scan leaf n219.
Padam names Kallua (Kalua) as one of the Bhatt poets and credits him with ten kabits titled 'Jhagra Hir Ranjhe ka', so title and author are both confirmed. Page 218 is scan leaf n221.
Padam describes Maha Singh as a nephew of Bhai Mani Singh who wrote in Anandpur, and prints the one devotional piece he found, expressing longing for the Guru. Page 224 is scan leaf n227.

Padam notes that works such as Hanuman Natak and Sur Sagar were copied into Gurmukhi at the Anandpur court, and reports that a copy written there in 1753 Bk (c. 1696) was preserved in the Sikh Reference Library, Amritsar.
Padam says Sur Sagar, among other texts, was copied into Gurmukhi for the Anandpur court. No Gurmukhi Sur Sagar manuscript was found online.

Excerpts from Lakhan Rai's Hitopadesh bhakha (1737 Bk / 1680) and Tansukh's version. Padam locates a Devanagari draft of Lakhan Rai's text at the Bhasha Vibhag Library, Patiala (MS no. 408), which has not been digitised.
Padam credits Prahilad Rai with the court's bhakha translation of the Upanishads (begun 1746 Bk) and compares it with Dara Shikoh's Sirr-i Akbar.

contains.note: Treatise on the names, haunts and capture of hunting birds, a hawking manual in the same family as the court animal manuals. The record names Maharaja Fatteh Singh as author and L. Hukam Chand as translator into English.

versions.notes: 167 ff. The record gives language as English and dates the item 1900; it does not say whether the leaves are the Gurmukhi original or the translation. Not related to the wanted Suan Nama (that is about dogs, this one about hawks).
